question: Can an attention map or individual weight matrix reliably identify the algorithm a transformer implements, even on a simple bounded Dyck grammar?

key_findings.claim: For a constrained two-layer Dyck transformer, optimal length generalization is characterized by a balance condition that allows many non-stack-like attention patterns, including uniform attention.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 gives a necessary-and-sufficient cancellation condition for matched bracket pairs under a minimal first layer; Corollary 1 constructs uniform-attention solutions, so an intuitive stack-shaped head is not required by the function.

key_findings.claim: The balance characterization is robust to approximate finite-length optima under explicit regularity assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 bounds each matched-pair balance violation relative to a prediction-separation quantity when loss is sufficiently near optimal and the second-layer projection is Lipschitz; a corollary extends it to vanishing weight decay.

key_findings.claim: A single local weight component can be shared by pruned subnetworks approximating functionally different transformers.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 uses a lottery-ticket-style construction: a wider random 4L-layer transformer contains a pruning that approximates any bounded L-layer target. Corollary 3 makes two approximating subnetworks coincide on a chosen weight matrix, defeating interpretation from that matrix alone.

key_findings.claim: Ordinary training finds diverse, mostly non-stack-like solutions, while regularizing the theoretically relevant global balance property improves length generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Two-layer one-head models reach at least 97% in-distribution accuracy, yet attention variation across 40 initializations is 2.20-2.27, near the random baseline 2.85. Contrastive balance regularization reduces violation and improves testing at lengths 400-500 versus training below 28.

method.core_idea: Characterize the full solution set for bounded-Dyck next-token prediction and use functional non-identifiability constructions plus controlled training to test myopic interpretation methods.
method.mechanism: Assume a minimal first layer encoding bracket type and depth, derive exact and approximate cancellation conditions on the second layer, prove a random-transformer pruning approximation theorem, train small Dyck transformers across seeds and embeddings, and regularize a contrastive proxy for balance violation.
assumptions: Bounded-depth Dyck next-token prediction is an informative sandbox for transformer interpretability.
The exact theory uses a two-layer model with a minimal first layer and squared loss.
Approximate balance additionally assumes Lipschitz projection functions and near-optimal population loss.
The pruning theorem's large random supernetwork and approximation bounds bear on practical local interpretation.

techniques.role: Derives the global cancellation property needed for correct bracket prediction.
Exhibits qualitatively different internal patterns with the same behavior.
Shows local weight agreement is compatible with different global functions.
Penalizes output changes caused by inserting matched bracket prefixes.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer, one-head transformers trained on Dyck-2,4 strings shorter than 28
evaluations.result: All reported models achieve at least 97%

evaluations.setting: Forty random initializations with and without positional encoding
evaluations.result: 2.20 with position and 2.27 without, versus random-attention 2.85

evaluations.setting: Length generalization to Dyck prefixes of length 400-500
evaluations.result: Lower violation correlates with better accuracy; contrastive regularization moves models toward both

limitations: The main functional characterization relies on a minimal first layer that already encodes bracket depth.
Theory uses bounded grammar depth, squared loss, small layer count, and simplified projection assumptions.
Synthetic Dyck parsing is far simpler and more enumerable than natural-language or multimodal computations.
The existence of non-identifiable solutions does not show that every circuit-level or causal method fails.
The lottery-ticket construction requires a much larger random transformer and may be far from trained-model scale.
failure_modes: A visually structured attention map can be incidental rather than necessary for the output.
Two runs can implement the same high-level behavior with attention patterns too different for direct head matching.
A local weight interpretation ignores compensating transformations elsewhere in the network.
Balance regularization may encode task knowledge unavailable for real-world behaviors whose invariances are unknown.
reusable_insights: Validate an interpretation against function-preserving alternatives, not only visual plausibility.
Derive task-level invariants and perturb them causally before assigning semantics to a component.
Use multiple seeds and architecture parameterizations to measure whether an alleged circuit is identifiable.
open_questions: Which multi-component causal analyses remain identifiable under transformer reparameterizations?
Can analogous global invariants be discovered automatically for real language-model behaviors?
How often do practical training biases select a small equivalence class despite broad representational non-uniqueness?

competitive_landscape.title: Attention is not Explanation
competitive_landscape.difference: Jain and Wallace show task predictions can coexist with adversarially different attention in NLP models; the reviewed paper supplies a formal-language solution-set characterization and length-generalization invariant.

competitive_landscape.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Brunner et al. prove attention weights are non-identifiable when sequence length exceeds head dimension and propose effective attention; the reviewed work connects non-identifiability to whole-network algorithms and local weights on Dyck.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention is not not Explanation
competitive_landscape.difference: Wiegreffe and Pinter argue attention can support explanation under calibrated tests and definitions; the reviewed work narrows its claim to the inability to reverse-engineer algorithms from isolated components and demonstrates functionally diverse optima.

competitive_landscape.title: Self-Attention Networks Can Process Bounded Hierarchical Languages
competitive_landscape.difference: Yao et al. construct small transformers that process bounded Dyck and motivate stack-like behavior; the reviewed paper shows those interpretable constructions are only a small part of the viable and empirically reached solution set.

novelty_assessment: The paper goes beyond generic warnings about attention by combining a necessary/sufficient task invariant, an approximate version, a local-weight non-identifiability theorem, and training evidence. Its conclusion is appropriately scoped to myopic methods: it does not invalidate whole-network causal interpretability, and its strongest theory depends on a highly structured Dyck setup.
reviewer_notes: Read the full main text and the proof appendices needed to check theorem assumptions and scope. Direct primary arXiv records on attention explanation, identifiability, and bounded-Dyck transformer constructions were checked on 2026-08-23.
